sampling_model.design: The fifteen pre/post pairs and four roles are fixed before outcomes; independent complete blocks are split by an outcome-independent rule into sixty disjoint role samples.
sampling_model.units: For pair \(\ell\) and role \(j\), \(n_{\ell j}\) block-level threshold indicators are observed, with \(n_{\ell j}/n\to\pi_{\ell j}>0\).
sampling_model.treatment: Roles are treated-pre, control-post, control-pre, and treated-post; normal-link distributional parallel trends and no anticipation identify the untreated treated-post distribution.
sampling_model.overlap: All role counts are independent by construction; inference for overlapping original blocks is outside this version.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Cell probabilities use the add-half estimator \(\widetilde r_{\ell j}=(K_{\ell j}+1/2)/(n_{\ell j}+1)\); no known nuisance probability is assumed.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Theorem 1 identifies the transformed-CDF counterfactual, while Assumption 5 requires a uniform positive transformed-density lower bound and Theorem 2 gives \(\sqrt N\) Gaussian weak convergence for DTT under that interior regularity.
The main theorem bounds the inverse Mills ratio on a half-plane, and its corollary bounds derivatives.
The paper proves monotonicity, complete monotonicity, and Turán-type inequalities for the Gaussian Mills ratio.
The paper derives second-order limits and characterizes standard-bootstrap failure for functionals with a zero first derivative.
Rare truncation experiments admit Gaussian or Poisson limits under different retained-count regimes.
Exact inversion gives finite-sample-valid intervals for continuous real functions of multinomial probability vectors, with a Monte Carlo computational approximation.

body.tldr: The published normal-link distributional-DiD identity and its Poisson rare-event shortcut agree on exactly two cancellation planes, but their complete discrepancy off those planes is governed by a new mixed inverse-Mills coefficient that ordinary interior delta methods do not control. The kernel is the cancellation-safe factorization and the open uniform common-cutoff coefficient question; resolving it yields pairwise and fifteen-pair Gaussian drift frontiers, while the bounded-count branch has a product-Poisson limit and finite-sample inference uses a finitely terminating rational outer interval with simultaneous coverage and rare-regime expected-diameter control.

project_justification.gap: The normal-link DTT identity is Djuazon and Tsyawo's published baseline. Their Assumption 5 requires a fixed positive lower bound on \(\phi(\Phi^{-1}(F_{gt}(y)))\), which is impossible on comparable-rarity arrays because \(\phi(q(\rho_n c_{\ell j,n}))\to0\). One-dimensional Mills bounds, Gaussian second-order delta methods, and generic multinomial inversion do not settle the mixed cancellation coefficient or its two exact planes.
project_justification.niche: A fixed collection of sparse panel event probabilities creates a regime in which functional-form error, cancellation distance, and sampling experiment type move jointly.
project_justification.fill: The project derives the exact factorization first, isolates the common-cutoff uniform bound as the open analytic kernel, and carries it through Gaussian and product-Poisson limits and certified finite-sample outer inference.

body.related_work: Djuazon and Tsyawo (2026) supply the causal counterfactual map as the published identification baseline, not as a novelty target. Their Assumption 5 requires \(\inf_{g,t,y}\phi(\Phi^{-1}(F_{gt}(y)))\ge1/C\), so it excludes every comparable-rarity sequence \(F=\rho_n c\to0\); their Theorem 2(c) gives the interior \(\sqrt N\) DTT limit whose fixed-threshold gradient is reproduced by the split-role influence function. Pinelis (2019) and Baricz (2008) supply inverse-Mills integral and sign tools that inform the mixed-coefficient argument. Chen and Fang (2019) explain why first-order degeneracy requires higher-order analysis in Gaussian experiments, while Marohn (2001) shows why bounded rare counts lead to a different Poisson experiment. Sachs, Gabriel, and Fay (2026) motivate exact inversion for nonlinear functions of discrete probabilities; the present rational outer construction is informed by that framework but makes no optimality comparison. Fernández-Val, Meier, van Vuuren, and Vella (2024) and Wooldridge (2023) establish that nonlinear link choice is substantive in DiD, and Roth and Sant'Anna (2023) place functional-form sensitivity within identification rather than presentation.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The literal statement that every all-full table with all \(n_j\le6\) must yield an empty retained list is false without a calibration restriction: for example, with \(n_j=1\) and \(\beta=1/2\), the admissible point \(p_j=1/4\) has deviance \(8\log4<16=8/\beta\). The formal theorem therefore states the exact sufficient inequality for empty-list behavior. This diagnostic does not affect all-zero retention or coverage. The global Lipschitz constant is deliberately enormous, so finite termination is a mathematical certificate rather than a practical runtime guarantee.
body.honest_scope: The causal identification identity is wholly published baseline. The exact signed-rectangle identity and its pointwise sign argument have a concrete proof architecture. The first-class open content is a single common-cutoff inverse-tail remainder with explicit constants over the whole coefficient box, including both cancellation planes; the Gaussian frontier depends on that result. The product-Poisson and rational-interval statements remain theorem tasks, not verified results. The design uses sixty disjoint outcome-independent block-role samples and does not establish validity for overlapping original blocks. The prescribed conservative aggregate interval must include zero in the published 37-treated-block application, so no finite-sample power claim is made. Fixed interior probabilities satisfy the finite-threshold version of Djuazon and Tsyawo's Assumption 5 and reduce, with the displayed split-role influence function, to their Theorem 2(c); comparable-rarity arrays violate that assumption because their normal-link densities vanish. Exact cancellation reduces to equality of the normal and Poisson maps for every admitted rarity level.
